newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss banks ask court to drop Holocaust lawsuits.
newsitem.headline: Swiss banks ask court to drop Holocaust lawsuits.

text.p: Switzerland's three biggest banks have petitioned a U.S. court to dismiss or delay lawsuits charging them with hoarding unclaimed deposits of Holocaust victims.
The class-action lawsuits seek billions of dollars in damages from Credit Suisse Group, Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS) and Swiss Bank Corp (SBC).
Attorneys for the banks, in a letter to Judge Edward Korman of the Eastern District of New York, said the banks had been and were still ready to discuss a settlement.
But some of the parties involved in the suit were no longer willing to delay legal proceedings while talks proceed.

"The letter proposes that because of the novel nature of the complaints, the Court should address the defendants' motions to dismiss or stay the cases," the attorneys for the banks said in a summary of a 16-page letter to the court released on Tuesday.
"The banks remain willing to discuss settlement. The banks are committed to resolving these problems in a positive way," the letter said.

"However, it now appears that there is no longer a consensus among the parties to stay these proceedings while discussions take place. Accordingly, it is necessary to address how these cases should proceed."

Claimants, who include Holocaust survivors and heirs, slave labourers under the Nazis, and the World Council of Orthodox Jewish Communities, allege the banks failed to hand back wealth left by Holocaust victims.
Class-action suits are those filed by plaintiffs in the belief they represent an entire class of potential claimants whose suits can be combined into one.
A federal court judge has given the banks until May 15 to respond to the complaints.

Swiss banks have faced sharp criticism for their conduct during World War Two. Jewish groups claim banks may be silently holding billions of dollars in wealth left by Hitler's victims and have stonewalled relatives trying to track it down.
Attorneys for the banks argued that the claims in these cases implicate the interests of sovereign governments and involve events that occurred outside the United States more than 50 years ago.
"Some major historical problems can better be addressed through cooperative efforts outside a courtroom than through the adversarial process of a trial," they said.

They noted that the banks and the Swiss government have taken a number of steps to address the allegations, including creating an independent panel to search for unclaimed wealth that may have escaped two previous audits.

The government has also established a commission of historians to probe neutral Switzerland's wartime role as a financial centre and has proposed selling part of its official gold reserves to finance a huge humanitarian fund.
Banks and other private businesses have also donated more than 265 million Swiss francs to a memorial fund that will support needy Holocaust victims.

"We think Swiss banks and Switzerland as a whole did quite a lot in the past few months and we think it would be much better to continue to do what we initiated," UBS spokeswoman Gertrud Erismann said.
